paragraphs.text: Black-green ( or BG ), also called Golgari , is an enemy color pair. Their central conflict is free will ( black ) vs. destiny ( green ). Black and green are the foremost graveyard colors, and black-green decks and mechanics tend to play in this space. The two colors share the evergreen keywords deathtouch , haste , flash , and indestructible . They are mutual allies of red ( ).

The core conflict between black and green is free will versus destiny. Black believes that individuals are free to choose their own path in life, while green believes everyone's role in life has been predetermined by the natural order. Another conflict is parasitism versus symbiosis: black takes what it wants from the world, while green lives in harmony with the ecosystem.

The black-green conflict is sometimes described as death versus life, but this is an aesthetic trapping more than a true philosophical conflict—like ice versus fire . In reality, both colors are concerned with the entire cycle of life and death. While black leans slightly more toward death and green toward life, both appreciate the cycle in its totality. Black is the color most willing to harness death as a tool, while green is the most accepting of death as part of the natural order. Many cards play up the death-versus-life aesthetics because of how difficult it is to communicate free will versus determinism on cards.

As a color pair, black-green wields the parasitic parts of nature, such as diseases and fungi. Unfettered growth becomes a tool of power, spreading and dominating. Black-green thrives in dark and unseen places; it is the antithesis of the clean, orderly society represented by white-blue . This parasitic growth can be hard to stop because it has so many component pieces; on the other hand, it can be hard for black-green to control.

Like their shared ally red , black and green are both inward-looking colors: black looks to its desires to determine its action, while green looks to its genetics. Black-green is concerned with self-actualization. It looks within itself to determine its natural strengths (green), then exploits those strengths to take what it wants (black). Black-green characters tend to fall into one of two categories. They use nature's tools in self-serving ways (black ends with green means), or they do whatever is necessary to protect the natural world—e.g., eco-terrorism (green ends with black means).
Black-green heroes include Vraska and Tyvar Kell while villains include Savra and Glissa .

Black and green have more mechanical overlap than almost any other color pair. Most notably, they are the best colors at interacting with the graveyard . Black and green can both return cards from the graveyard, use the graveyard as a resource, and care about death triggers . Black-green decks, therefore, tend to be slow and grindy, generating card advantage by recycling their graveyards. While the design space for graveyard mechanics is deep, most sets don't want large amounts of graveyard synergies, which can make black-green a difficult color pair to design for.
The following mechanics are shared by black and green.
Consume Strength - combines green's "pump" effect with black's "weakness" effect onto a very efficient instant
Putrefy - combines green's dislike of artifacts with black's creature destruction onto one card with no drawback (i.e. cannot target black creatures)
Mark Rosewater (July 17, 2015). " #245 - Black/Green ". Drive to Work .
